Open Robotics ROS 2 sros2 load_policy XML External Entity Processing Information Disclosure Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of Open Robotics ROS 2. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of policy XML files. Due to the improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) references, a crafted document specifying a URI causes the XML parser to access the URI and embed the contents back into the XML document for further processing. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the current user. Was ZDI-CAN-32121.

codebase-memory-mcp provides local code intelligence for developers and AI agents through a persistent graph and MCP tools. Prior to 0.10.0, the indexer's .gitignore matcher implemented * and ** through recursive backtracking without a work bound. A repository containing a pattern with repeated wildcard groups and a long path could make matching work grow exponentially, allowing a single ignore rule to stall discovery indefinitely and, before worker isolation, stall the server. The impact is limited to availability, and the bounded matcher does not claim that every expensive input is eliminated. This issue is fixed in version 0.10.0.

codebase-memory-mcp provides local code intelligence for developers and AI agents through a persistent graph and MCP tools. Prior to 0.9.1-rc.1, the optional graph UI's POST /api/process-kill route omitted the indexing-job ownership check on Windows while retaining that check on POSIX systems. A requester able to reach the optional UI could supply an arbitrary process identifier, causing TerminateProcess to stop any process that the server user was permitted to terminate. The flaw affects the Windows-specific process termination path and can cause a high availability impact without disclosing or modifying data. This issue is fixed in version 0.9.1-rc.1.

codebase-memory-mcp provides local code intelligence for developers and AI agents through a persistent graph and MCP tools. Prior to 0.9.0, the detect_changes tool validated the base_branch argument for shell metacharacters but omitted the leading-dash check before placing the value in the revision position of a git diff command. Git therefore interpreted an option-shaped base_branch value, including --output, as a command option instead of a revision, allowing a caller to create or overwrite a caller-chosen file with Git diff output under the server process's permissions. Arbitrary code execution was not demonstrated. This issue is fixed in version 0.9.0.

Avahi is a system which facilitates service discovery on a local network via the mDNS/DNS-SD protocol suite. In 0.9-rc4 and earlier, org.freedesktop.Avahi.Server.RecordBrowserNew accepts a domain-name value that avahi_is_valid_domain_name considers valid even though avahi_normalize_name_strdup cannot normalize it. The resulting null key reaches the key assertion in dbus_prepare_record_browser_object. A local low-privileged D-Bus client can trigger the mismatch and terminate the Avahi daemon, causing denial of service. The issue is fixed in 0.9-rc5.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the edit_modinput_data_migrator capability could cause the data migration input to run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands with elevated permissions. With this access, the user could read data outside the assigned role scope and write data to indexes and lookup tables.
The vulnerability is possible because the data migration input does not restrict configured searches to product-supplied migration tasks before it runs them with elevated permissions.
For more information see Capability reference for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/capability-reference-for-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.9.4 until 3.10.4, NLTK corpus-reader path pointers and view methods validate a requested relative path without consistently resolving intermediate directory symlinks against the reader's scoped root. A local attacker who can place such a symlink can make abspaths or words reach a readable file outside the corpus root and disclose its contents. On releases with pathsec enforcement, the file must remain inside a global NLTK allowed root; version 3.9.4 has enforcement disabled and permits a broader escape. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. Prior to 3.10.4, WordNet Synset.max_depth, min_depth, hypernym_paths, and hypernym_distances recursively follow attacker-controlled corpus pointers without a visited-node set or depth cap. A cyclic or excessively deep hypernym graph can raise RecursionError and terminate traversal APIs and similarity operations that depend on them. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

cassandra-jdbc-wrapper provides a JDBC-compliant API over the Java driver for Apache Cassandra. Prior to 4.16.4 and 5.0.2, DriverUtil.toStringWithoutSensitiveValues() and DriverUtil.redactSensitiveValuesInJdbcUrl() redact the password property but not the equally sensitive token property used for DataStax Astra and other token-based authentication. When DEBUG logging is enabled, SessionHolder passes connection properties and JDBC URLs containing token through these helpers, causing the live token to be written in plaintext when connections are acquired or released. An attacker who can read those logs can use the token to access Cassandra data and operations authorized to that credential. This issue is fixed in versions 4.16.4 and 5.0.2.

A weakness has been identified in Directus up to 12.6.1. Affected by this issue is the function getSecret of the file api/src/services/shares.ts of the component Share Login Service. This manipulation causes incorrect authorization. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been made available to the public and could be used for attacks. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure.

The rsyslog's`imuxsock` special parser can end up writing into the received message raw buffer when trying to replace the message timestamp with the system's timestamp. A local attacker with the ability to write to the `imuxsock` socket can leverage that by crafting a malformed PRI value with a short timestamp to lead the rsyslog to perform the out-of-bounds write.

A flaw was found in ansible-core. When a task or its parameters are marked no_log: true, sensitive values passed to a module's warn() or deprecate() calls are not redacted and are printed in cleartext to stdout/stderr in warning and deprecation messages. The 'warnings' and 'deprecations' keys are retained in the PRESERVE allow-list in lib/ansible/_internal/_task.py when the task result is censored, so sensitive parameters bypass masking and can be disclosed in output captured in terminal sessions, CI logs, and any automation wrapping ansible-playbook, even though every task touching the secrets is marked no_log: true.

The GPTranslate – Multilingual AI Translation Agent for WordPress: Translate Your Site with AI plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 2.34.17 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Exploitation requires the plugin's non-default 'HTML DOM method' to be enabled for server-side translation, and a translation row for the target language-prefixed URL must exist to arm the output buffer that routes page content through the vulnerable Simple HTML DOM parser.

The Real Cookie Banner: GDPR & ePrivacy Cookie Consent plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 5.4.2 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Exploitation requires that the cookie banner has been activated by the site administrator (the plugin's primary onboarding step) and that at least one prior comment from the same name and email identity has already been approved, after which WordPress core's comment_previously_approved default auto-approves subsequent comments without administrator action.

The Speed Booster Pack ⚡ PageSpeed Optimization Suite plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'author' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 4.5.9.1 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Exploitation requires that the plugin's Lazy load media option is enabled and that the attacker's comment is approved by a site administrator or via auto-approval.

The WP Data Access – App Builder for Tables, Forms, Dashboards, Charts & Maps plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'HyperlinkObject.label (percent-encoded)' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 5.5.92 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. This requires the WordPress site to have a published Anonymous-access Registration Form app configured against a table with a HyperlinkObject column, and a legacy Data Project list using a $$link$$ Dynamic Hyperlink against that same column; given this configuration, any unauthenticated visitor can plant the payload.

The Redux Framework plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the '<opt_name>[<color-field-id>]' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 4.5.17 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The wp_kses_post() sanitization applied via Redux_Helpers::sanitize_array() is bypassed — not broken — because an <a class="thickbox" title="&lt;img onerror=...&gt;"> payload uses only kses-allowed tags and attributes, with the entity-encoded onerror handler surviving storage as inert text that the browser decodes when WordPress core's thickbox.js reads the title attribute and writes it into the modal as HTML. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

The ShortPixel Image Optimizer – Optimize Images, Convert WebP & AVIF plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 6.6.1 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Exploitation requires the administrator to have enabled the 'Deliver WebP/AVIF images using the ShortPixel CDN' (useCDN) option, after which any unauthenticated visitor can submit a comment containing a crafted url() payload inside an allowed HTML construct such as <acronym title="...">, which WordPress comment kses preserves on save; the dangerous attribute-boundary breakout occurs only at render time inside the ob_start output-buffer rewriter, where kses does not apply.

The MailerLite – Signup forms (official) plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'form_id' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.7.27 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. This requires an administrator to approve a comment containing the malicious shortcode, after which any page rendering the Latest Comments block with excerpts enabled will trigger the injected script for all visitors.

The Social Media Auto Poster – Schedule & Publish to Buffer plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 6.2.9. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to delete Buffer sync log history for and disclose Buffer sync log contents of arbitrary posts, including those authored by administrators. The nonce used as the sole gate is not bound to any specific post ID, so a nonce harvested from the attacker's own draft editor screen is valid against any arbitrary post ID submitted in the request.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When processing token requests using the User-Managed Access (UMA) grant, Keycloak fails to verify whether a target client or resource server is enabled before issuing an authorization token. An authenticated remote user can exploit this flaw to obtain valid Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for disabled clients, bypassing administrative access controls and permissions restrictions.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability allows an authenticated remote attacker to cause a denial of service by terminating active sessions of arbitrary users. When processing Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) documents that lack a root signature, Keycloak accepts the request as long as any assertion within the document is signed, without verifying its context or placement. An attacker holding a validly signed assertion can embed it into an unsigned logout request for another user, causing Keycloak to accept the forged request and terminate the victim's session.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could store attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) in a shared data model.
The vulnerability is possible because the Data Model Editor does not properly neutralize data model field names when it builds a preview search.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The attacker should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Add a regular expression field (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/manage-knowledge-objects/knowledge-management-manual/10.4/define-data-model-dataset-fields/add-a-regular-expression-field), Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities), and About the search language (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/search/search-manual/10.4/search-overview/about-the-search-language) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to author and run playbooks could add messages to a different playbook run log and cause that run to fail, including runs outside the labels that the user could access.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not verify that playbook API requests use the trusted runtime context for the current playbook run.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with container edit permission could supply timestamps when creating containers and artifacts through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. This could alter the timeline shown to analysts and cause configured data retention strategies to delete affected records earlier than intended.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API accepts client-supplied values for timestamps that Splunk SOAR uses to order records and apply data retention.
The early deletion impact requires an applicable data retention strategy; the timeline impact does not.
For more information see Manage your PostgreSQL database with data retention strategies (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/6.4.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-system-health-and-performance/manage-your-postgresql-database-with-data-retention-strategies) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to create and view containers for a label could use the Representational State Transfer (REST) API to create a container that references a workbook phase in a case the user cannot view, disclosing the phase name and creating an inconsistent phase association.
The vulnerability exists because the Container REST API does not enforce the same case-scoped authorization when it accepts a workbook-phase reference during container creation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to view and edit containers and at least one container label could set misleading user and app provenance on containers that the user creates and learn whether user IDs and installed app identifiers exist.
The vulnerability is possible because the Representational State Transfer (REST) API accepts client-supplied values for server-managed container fields.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to create containers on one label could use the Representational State Transfer (REST) API to create a container with a parent relationship to a container that the user cannot access. This could let the user alter incident lineage across authorization boundaries and identify existing restricted containers.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API accepts a customer-supplied parent relationship when creating a container without authorizing access to the referenced container.
For more information see REST Containers (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/8.6.0/container-endpoints/rest-containers) and Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to edit containers for an allowed label could forge the author attribution of container pins and access limited user details outside the expected authorization boundary.
The Container Pin Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not prevent caller-provided author fields from reaching generic model binding, which lets the request reassign a pin author or query user-related data outside the expected authorization scope.
For more information see Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/6.3.1/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in data used by the Weak Encrypted Communication report. If another user who can access the report selects an affected drilldown, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the drilldown. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the drilldown.
The vulnerability is possible because the Weak Encrypted Communication report does not validate source, destination, and Secure Sockets Layer version values before inserting them into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Weak Encrypted Communication (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/installation-and-configuration-manual/8.7/configure-reports/weak-encrypted-communication) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in endpoint summary data. If another user who can access the Time Center dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Time Center dashboard does not safely escape endpoint summary values before inserting them into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Endpoint dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/endpoint-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in managed-lookup audit data. If another user who can access the Managed Lookups Audit dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Managed Lookups Audit dashboard does not safely escape audit data before inserting it into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Audit dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/audit-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in vulnerability data. If another user who can access the Vulnerability Search dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Vulnerability Search dashboard encodes data-model field values for the drilldown link but does not escape the values as SPL search literals before inserting the values into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Network dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/network-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user who holds the "ess_user" Splunk Enterprise Security role could run a search that causes attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) text to appear in the Search Audit dashboard. If another user who can access the dashboard selects the affected search, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled SPL commands using the permissions of the user who selects the search. The user who runs the first search could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the affected search.
The vulnerability is possible because the Search Audit dashboard does not safely escape logged search text before inserting it into drilldown searches.
For more information see Users and roles for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/users-and-roles-for-splunk-enterprise-security) and Audit dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/audit-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in the Malware data model. Another authenticated user with access to the Malware Search dashboard could later select a table row containing those values. Splunk Enterprise Security could then run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selected the row. The commands could expose data available to the user who selected the row and add attacker-controlled records to an index.
The vulnerability is possible because the Malware Search dashboard does not safely quote row values before adding them to drilldown searches.
For more information see Endpoint dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.4/analytics/endpoint-dashboards) and Users and roles for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/users-and-roles-for-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, an authenticated user who does not hold the edit_correlationsearches capability could set Status to Testing for a versioned detection or clear that setting. This could affect the integrity and availability of detection testing.
The vulnerability is possible because the Test Mode Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not require the edit_correlationsearches capability before it creates or deletes scheduled test copies of detections.
For more information see Capability reference for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/capability-reference-for-splunk-enterprise-security) and Test detections on production data using Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.7/detections/test-detections-on-production-data-using-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user who holds the "ess_user" Splunk Enterprise Security role could store attacker-controlled asset data in an asset source lookup. A user that holds a role with the mc_assets_read capability could later open the Asset Center dashboard and select that value in the Asset Information table. Splunk Enterprise Security could then run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of that user. With this access, the user who stored the asset data could expose or modify data available to the user who selected the value.
The vulnerability is possible because Asset Center does not escape asset values before adding them to drilldown searches.
The vulnerability requires Asset Center to process the asset data and another user to select the value. The user who stored the data should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Users and roles for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/users-and-roles-for-splunk-enterprise-security), Add asset and identity data to Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.7/asset-and-identity-management/add-asset-and-identity-data-to-splunk-enterprise-security), and Asset and identity dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/asset-and-identity-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could inject arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands into a Classic Dashboard search. When another user opens the affected dashboard in Splunk Web, those injected commands execute with the viewing user's permissions, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to access stored credentials and write data to indexes.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape user-supplied content when it rewrites a search, which lets the rewritten search include additional SPL commands.
The vulnerability requires another user to open the dashboard in Splunk Web. Consequently, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) and Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could make unauthorized changes when restoring archived indexed data or cause a Denial of Service (DoS) on the Splunk Enterprise instance.
The vulnerability is possible because the Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not require the indexes_edit capability for archived-data restoration actions.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.
For more information see Restore archived indexed data (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-indexers-and-indexer-clusters/10.6/back-up-and-archive-your-indexes/restore-archived-indexed-data) in the Splunk documentation.

Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to 7.3.0, the six network address set handlers in cmd/incusd/network_address_sets.go resolved the effective project with project.NetworkProject(), which returns default when features.networks is unset. The expandProject authorization switch in cmd/incusd/daemon.go omitted auth.ObjectTypeNetworkAddressSet, so authorization used the requested project instead of the effective project. This issue is fixed in version 7.3.0.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. An authenticated remote user with a pending required security action, such as configuring multi-factor authentication (MFA), can bypass the mandatory action by submitting a specially crafted request to the consent endpoint without a valid session code. Keycloak incorrectly interprets the submission as a page refresh and completes the authentication process, allowing the user to access the application without fulfilling the required security policies.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. Prior to 3.10.4, nltk.classify.weka.ARFF_Formatter writes attacker-controlled class labels into the Weka ARFF @ATTRIBUTE '-label-' declaration without safely formatting the label tokens. Crafted labels can alter the generated ARFF schema or records, corrupting classifier input and causing integrity loss or processing failure. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

A flaw was found in Moodle. Insufficient authorization checks in the quiz editing functionality allow an authenticated user with teacher privileges to view slot details and modify sections of quizzes they do not have permission to manage. An attacker could exploit this flaw to alter quiz configurations or disclose quiz structure information without proper authorization.

A flaw was found in Moodle. Due to a missing authorization check when editing Lesson activity pages, authenticated users with teacher privileges can view and move lesson pages from courses they are not permitted to access into their own lessons. This issue can lead to unauthorized access and modification of restricted course content.

A flaw was found in Moodle. Missing authorization checks in the forum discussion web services allow authenticated users to view discussion information in courses they do not have permission to access. In addition, users with teacher privileges may lock forum discussions in courses where they lack proper authorization. This issue can lead to unauthorized information disclosure and unauthorized discussion state modification.

A flaw was found in Moodle. Due to missing ownership checks in badge alignments, an authenticated user with badge management privileges can view and modify alignments associated with badges they do not own. This vulnerability can lead to unauthorized data disclosure and tampering with badge configurations.

A flaw was found in Moodle. Missing ownership verification in Feedback activity templates allows an authenticated teacher to view, use, or delete templates associated with courses other than their own. This can result in unauthorized access, modification, or deletion of course materials.

Open OnDemand is an open-source high-performance computing portal. Prior to 4.1.6 and 4.2.3, apps/dashboard/config/initializers/session_store.rb stores dashboard sessions by default in a predictable /var/tmp/<username> directory, or in another location configured by an administrator, but omits PUN user directory ownership and mode 0700 validation. A local attacker can pre-create another user's directory, read the victim's session identifier and CSRF token after login, or stage a predetermined session identifier. ActiveSupport file-store deserialization of attacker-controlled cache data may also occur in the victim's context, enabling file modification or code execution with the victim's privileges. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.6 and 4.2.3.

Chamilo LMS is an open-source learning management system. Prior to 2.0.3, POST /api/social_posts accepts attacker-controlled content that SocialPost::setContent stores without cross-site scripting sanitization, and assets/vue/components/social/SocialWallPost.vue renders post.content through v-html without sanitization. Any authenticated user can create a social-wall post that executes active content when another authenticated user views the wall. The script can run in an administrator's browser session and expose session data or perform actions with the victim's privileges. This issue is fixed in version 2.0.3.

Chamilo LMS is an open-source learning management system. Prior to 1.11.40 and 2.0.3, main/lp/scormItem.class.php and public/main/lp/scormItem.class.php store an attacker-controlled title element from imsmanifest.xml without cross-site scripting sanitization when a teacher imports a SCORM package. The title reaches c_lp_item.title and is rendered by src/CoreBundle/Resources/views/LearnPath/scorm_list.html.twig through item.title with raw output while Twig auto-escaping is disabled; the default configuration does not apply the optional AI-disclosure sanitization path. Enrolled students or administrators who view the learning-path table of contents can execute the stored content in their browser sessions. This issue is fixed in versions 1.11.40 and 2.0.3.
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2026.1.3 improper authorization allowed project viewers to change project IDs

The Link Library plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'linkfile[name]' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 7.10.0 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. This requires an administrator to have enabled the "Link File" option within the plugin's settings, which activates the vulnerable file upload field on the public add-link form.
An issue in PHPGurukul Employee Leaves Management System (ELMS) Version 2.1 allows a remote attacker to escalate privileges via the PHP session management mechanism

Dell PowerStore contains a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability. A low-privileged authenticated attacker could exploit this vulnerability, potentially leading to execution of malicious script in a higher-privileged user's session.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a code injection vulnerability in the MAGICK, XBM, XPM and UIL encoders that allows local attackers to inject content via crafted filenames. Attackers with access to the output directory and control over the filename can inject additional headers or code into the generated image source output.

The HivePress – Business Directory, Listings & Classified Ads Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'description' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.8.1 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

The Asset CleanUp: Page Speed Booster plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.4.0.6 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The exploit succeeds even though wp_kses is applied on save, because the XSS is manufactured post-sanitization by the plugin's regex pass: kses-permitted tags such as <a title> and <code> carry the attacker's marker and terminator strings intact into the rendered HTML buffer, where the plugin's own replacement then corrupts the document structure.

The BuddyPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Insecure Direct Object Reference in all versions up to, and including, 14.4.0. This is due to the `get_item_permissions_check` function in the Messages REST API endpoint trusting a client-supplied `user_id` parameter instead of using the authenticated user's ID. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers with Subscriber-level access and above to read, update, or delete other users' private message threads by specifying the victim's user ID in the request.

Daptin before 0.13.61 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users to overwrite restricted contacts by sending CardDAV PUT requests to existing contacts. Attackers holding address book Update permission can bypass per-contact row permissions in PutAddressObject to modify protected contacts and confirm their existence.

A vulnerability was determined in MaysWind AriaNg-Native up to 1.3.14. Affected by this issue is the function shell.openPath of the file main/ipc/main-process.js of the component IPC Handler. This manipulation of the argument dir causes improper input validation. The attack can be initiated remotely. Upgrading to version 1.3.15 can resolve this issue. Patch name: ac5a4bcf102f605b160f19fcc9fbaec67f9596d7. You should upgrade the affected component.

AutoGPT is a workflow automation platform for creating, deploying, and managing continuous artificial intelligence agents. From 0.6.63 before 0.11.0, the Office preview expands an embedded ZIP thumbnail without a size limit. A signed-in user with access to workspace file previews can exhaust the memory of a platform API worker with one small crafted DOCX, XLSX, or PPTX file and one preview request. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.0.

A vulnerability was identified in Dispatcharr up to 0.32.0. Affected by this issue is the function get_permissions of the component VODLogoViewSet/M3UAccountViewSet. Such manipulation leads to incorrect authorization. The attack may be launched remotely. Upgrading to version 0.33.0 can resolve this issue. The name of the patch is ac7a23cc584761b88f8d87dd8ac3688426024ed8. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component.

LiteLLM Secret Manager oidc Resolver Information Disclosure Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of LiteLLM. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the secret resolution handler. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied input prior to using it to access environment variables. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the service account. Was ZDI-CAN-31482.

A weakness has been identified in GongShengyue OnlineBooks up to dfc5eacc08d3b0396c266049548618f6fb9587ea. Impacted is an unknown function. This manipulation causes cross-site request forgery. The attack is possible to be carried out remotely. This product adopts a rolling release strategy to maintain continuous delivery. Therefore, version details for affected or updated releases cannot be specified. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

AutoGPT is a workflow automation platform for creating, deploying, and managing continuous artificial intelligence agents. In versions 0.6.1 through 0.10.0, credentials are sent to a third party when a redirect's Location header hides the new host behind a backslash. A signed-in user who connects an MCP server URL, or runs a shared or marketplace workflow with a host-scoped credential, can have that credential delivered to a third party if the host responds with a redirect whose Location the other party influenced. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.0.

browser-use before 1.0.0 contains a URL parser differential vulnerability in SecurityWatchdog that allows attackers to bypass allowed_domains, prohibited_domains, and block_ip_addresses checks by crafting a URL with a backslash before the allowed host, exploiting the mismatch between urllib.parse hostname extraction and Chromium's WHATWG-style URL parsing. Attackers can influence an LLM-controlled navigate action, such as through prompt injection, to send requests to loopback or private addresses or arbitrary external hosts before the browser redirects to about:blank, enabling SSRF and persistent state changes on the target server.

Obtainium before 1.7.5 contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows remote attackers to write or delete JSON files outside app_data by supplying an app id containing ../ sequences. Attackers can serve an obtainium://app deep link with a crafted id that, once imported, overwrites other app configurations or writes files to shared storage, and later deletes them on app removal.

Marley through 16.8.1 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows authenticated patient-portal users to create payment records against other patients' documents by supplying arbitrary patient and docname values. Attackers can call the get_payment_link endpoint, which saves Healthcare Payment Records with ignore_permissions, to corrupt another patient's payment history and reconciliation data.

Joomla! Core - [20261137] - Core - Improper access checks in com_content vote task in Joomla 1.6.0-5.4.10, 6.0.0-6.2.0 - Missing access checks in the vote task allowed users to rate articles they are not allowed to see, including unpublished articles.

GPAC through 26.07.0 contains a heap out-of-bounds read vulnerability in gf_rtp_parse_amr that allows remote RTP senders or malicious RTSP servers to read beyond packet buffers by sending crafted AMR/AMR-WB payloads. Attackers can send short packets whose TOC entries all set the F bit, causing out-of-bounds frame data to be copied into decoder output, disclosing memory or crashing the client.

GPAC through 26.07.0 contains a heap out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the STAP-A handling of gf_rtp_parse_h264 in rtp_depacketizer.c due to unchecked aggregation unit sizes. A malicious RTP sender or RTSP server can send STAP-A packets with oversized NAL unit lengths to disclose adjacent heap memory or crash the client.

plugNmeet-server before 2.5.3 contains an authorization flaw in PollsController.HandleUserSubmitResponse that allows authenticated room participants to submit poll votes as other users by supplying an arbitrary UserId. Attackers can set UserId to another participant's id to cast votes on their behalf or block their legitimate votes, manipulating poll results.

HarnessRouter 0.4.2 before 0.32.2 contains an open redirect vulnerability in the self-hosted sign-in UI that allows unauthenticated attackers to redirect users via the unvalidated next query parameter. Attackers can send crafted login links with an external, protocol-relative, or backslash-prefixed next value so victims are sent to attacker sites after signing in, enabling phishing.

Movary before 0.78.0 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows authenticated non-admin users to make the server request internal hosts by submitting crafted Jellyfin or Plex server URLs. Attackers can target internal services directly since URL validation is disabled by default, or bypass it via DNS rebinding, redirects, or AAAA records to probe internal network state.

Listdom by Webilia plugin for WordPress before 6.5.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated attackers with Contributor-level access or above to retrieve the email address and user ID of every registered user. Attackers can exploit the LSD_Ajax::autosuggest() handler by setting the source parameter to users and repeating requests with different term values to enumerate the full user base, including administrators, bypassing the 10-result limit.

Insert Pages plugin for WordPress (insert-pages) before 3.11.6 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability in the insert_pages_handle_shortcode_insert() function that allows authenticated attackers with Contributor-level access or above to read draft, pending, scheduled, and private posts they do not own. Attackers can reference sequential post IDs in the [insert page] shortcode to render the full content, title, excerpt, and metadata of unpublished posts, since the function checks a generic read capability instead of enforcing the read_post meta capability tied to post author and status.

Wallabag from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 2.6.16 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users to annotate other users' entries by referencing global entry IDs. The issue is fixed in Metasploit Framework 6.5.10

When the parent of an embed tag was an expression other than a string or a variable, the sandbox didn't see that expression. The functions, filters and tests of the expression weren't checked against the policy, and neither were its conversions to strings. A sandboxed template allowed to use embed could therefore call any function, filter or test, and any __toString() method:

{% embed 'leak_' ~ app_secret() %}{% endembed %}

Method calls and property reads were not affected, since they're checked at runtime.

The sandbox now checks the parent expression of embed like any other expression of the template.

The sandbox checks that a template may call toString() on an object before converting it to a string. For an object, the is true test evaluates to the object itself, and that result wasn't checked. A sandboxed template could therefore print an object through a denied toString() method:

{{ obj is true }}

The same applies when the result is concatenated or passed to a filter. No tag needs to be allowed. A test in a boolean context, like {% if obj is true %}, isn't affected, since it doesn't convert the object to a string.

The sandbox now checks the result of tests like the result of filters and functions.
